pattern_stance_changes.reason: The only comparison is v1 against v2, and v1 is itself a developer-defined pipeline (ReAct+RAG with the planner as a tool, then one monolithic generation call), not an open agent loop. v2 changes five things at once: a fixed first planner call, update-plan, three fixed generation stages, new retrieval sources and a programmatic fix. There is no ablation, and v1 is not a same-budget alternative, since v2 uses 2.4-4.0x the input tokens (mistral-small 23,914 to 94,505; granite 47,371 to 117,594; Tables II-III). Neither the structural gains nor the gpt-oss semantic regression can be attributed to the fixed graph, so under the stance rule this is use without an isolating comparison. Labelling it mixed would count the paper toward 'contested' on equally unattributable evidence in both directions.

Moving the planner from an in-loop tool to a fixed first call is credited as the key change but is bundled with the other four v2 changes and the 2.4-4.0x larger context, with no ablation. There is no isolating comparison either way, so the evidence is not mixed; the pattern is used.

missed_issues: The semantic grading count does not add up. 1,044 gradings = 348 cells x 3 runs, and §VI-B says only structurally valid runs were graded, but granite v1 has 73 and mistral-small v1 77 structurally valid runs (Table II), fewer than the 87 needed for three per prompt. Some v1 cells were therefore graded on fewer than three runs, on invalid runs, or not at all, and the paper does not say how prompts with zero valid runs enter the 29-prompt mean and SE. This bears directly on mistral-small's +19.8, the largest semantic gain.

The corruption filter keeps runs of at least 40% of the largest valid run in the same cell, so it is relative to the cell. A cell in which every run is a stub passes it, so the filter cannot catch the stub failure mode that drives gpt-oss-120b's collapse.

llama-3.3-70b's generation rate fell from 95.3% to 81.5% (221 to 189 of 232) on v2, which the paper itself calls unexplained (§V, §VII-B). Together with the gpt-oss stubs, that is a second model-specific regression under the same pipeline change. The review's summary reads as uniform gains on that pipeline-level metric.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats and with all claim strengths. The quadrant miscount is real: three models, not four, meet >90% and <60 s in Table III. Blind, I put COI at medium because the paper reports unflattering results (at most 55.2% satisfaction, the gpt-oss collapse), but REVIEW_RUBRIC line 38 makes a vendor evaluating its own product without independent replication high, so the review's high stands. My disagreement is with the P36 and P13 stances. The paper shows that a heavier, staged, retrieval-rich pipeline beats a lighter pipeline on schema validity for six mid-size models at 2.4-4.0x the tokens. It does not show that a static graph beats an agent loop. Its transferable evidence is about gates: schema validity can rise while task satisfaction collapses.
